sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The alder is a sacred tree of the Celts. It belongs to the genus Alnus. Its branches carry tiny cones and dangling catkins at the same time. The Celts read this as a sign that the seasons of past and future meet. They tied the alder to divination and to foretelling, and the link lasted into early modern Scotland. Fresh alder wood turns from white to red, as a wound does. The old Celts saw the change as a living spirit, so they made the felling of an alder a kind of murder. The Fairy folk hid their theft of cattle behind alder boughs, leaving the branches in the place of the beasts. In Wales the hero Brân the Blessed carried an alder branch, and the poet Gwydion knew him by it.

okr.objective: Record the alder, a Celtic sacred tree.
key_results: Show the tree, its magic, and its ties to Brân and Gwydion.
